{"id": "6:52/q09", "question": "Does 'His face' imply a bodily part?", "turns_on": "Whether face is read figuratively, as a divine attribute, or as a bodily part.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q09/p1", "position": "No; face is an Arabic metonym or metaphor for essence, aspect, direction, favor, or what brings one near God.", "reasons": "Jishumi notes bodily and figurative senses in Arabic. Razi answers the anthropomorphists with God's oneness in 112:1; Abu Hayyan rejects their inference. Tabataba'i denies body and material direction, takes 55:27's grammatical modifier with face, and uses 28:88 and other verses for enduring nearness of divine attributes and righteous realities. Qushayri and Alusi discuss the difficulty of willing God's eternal essence when will ordinarily attaches to originated or possible things. Ibn Qutayba treats 'His face' as an expression for seeking God in supplication; Damghani and the exegetes reported by Ibn al-Jawzi understand it as God Himself or His pleasure."}, {"id": "6:52/q09/p2", "position": "It may be understood as God's possessed Face or literal sight of it.", "reasons": "Qurtubi records that God is described as possessing the Face, citing 55:27 and 13:22; StudyQuran reports Razi's lover analogy as literal hope to see it. Razi reports anthropomorphists' bodily argument only to refute it."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q10", "question": "How does 'seeking His face' attach grammatically?", "turns_on": "Whether the circumstantial clause qualifies the worshippers or the object of their calling.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q10/p1", "position": "It is a circumstantial clause qualifying the callers' supplication and sincerity.", "reasons": "Qushayri, Abu Hayyan, Bursevi and Ibn Ashur identify the ḥāl; Bursevi calls sincerity central. Samin prefers attachment to the subject of يدعون, with an implicit 'through their supplication at those times.'"}, {"id": "6:52/q10/p2", "position": "It could be a circumstance of the object of يدعون.", "reasons": "Samin records this possible grammatical attachment but prefers the subject."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q11", "question": "Whose account is meant by the reciprocal pronouns?", "turns_on": "Whether the nearest antecedent governs both clauses or the clauses parenthetically address concern for the chiefs' conversion.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q11/p1", "position": "The poor worshippers' account and the Prophet's account.", "reasons": "The nearest explicit group and the later object 'expel them' favor this for Wahidi, Razi, Abu Hayyan, Samin and Kuranyolu. Al-Mahdawi says all pronouns refer to believers; Alusi cites Ata and most commentators."}, {"id": "6:52/q11/p2", "position": "The first reciprocal pronouns refer to the polytheists; the later 'expel them' refers to believers.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's version assigns reward and punishment to God; Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya, Razi, Baydawi, Alusi and Islahi say the Prophet need not court pagan conversion. StudyQuran reports this as more plausible, while other sources prefer the believers by proximity. Samin notes parenthesis need not depend on this referent."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q12", "question": "What is the 'account' for which neither side is responsible?", "turns_on": "Whether حساب is moral reckoning, provision/sufficiency, or the disbelievers' responsibility for faith.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q12/p1", "position": "The reckoning of deeds, faith and hidden intentions belongs to each person and ultimately God.", "reasons": "Hasan and the majority take deeds; Noah's reply at 26:112–113 and the rule that no bearer bears another's burden support this. Zamakhshari, Razi, Biqai and Bursawi say the Prophet judges outward piety, even against a claim that the poor seek food and clothes. Abu Hayyan rejects positing actual inward blame after God's testimony; Ibn Ashur likewise finds no sound report of hypocrisy and rejects treating both clauses as merely divine accounting. Asad extends personal accountability to differing belief and conduct. Elmalılı says the Prophet should not expel them on a pretext of having to account for them."}, {"id": "6:52/q12/p2", "position": "It means worldly provision or sufficiency: neither the Prophet nor the poor believers must provide for the other.", "reasons": "Tabari, Ibn Bahr and others say fear of maintaining the poor cannot justify expulsion; God provides for both. Ibn Bahr and Biqai cite 78:36 for ample gift; Biqai adds 2:212, Abu Ubayd and Ibn Faris for aḥsabtuhu 'gave enough,' and a report on hospitality. Kuranyolu phrases the practical result as not sending worshippers away to earn a living."}, {"id": "6:52/q12/p3", "position": "It is the chiefs' own response to faith, for which the Prophet is not liable.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas's alternative and Ibn Ashur/Islahi say eagerness for conversion cannot cost existing believers their rights. Ibn Ashur also allows 'their account' to mean the chiefs' reckoning of the believers' poverty."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q13", "question": "Why are both reciprocal account clauses stated?", "turns_on": "Whether repetition supplies reciprocal completeness alone or also exposes the requesters' false rationale.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q13/p1", "position": "Together they state complete reciprocity: neither party bears the other's account.", "reasons": "Zamakhshari, Razi and others say both halves complete one point, invoking the no-burden rule. Bursawi reports Abu al-Suud that the uncontroversial reverse reinforces the first; Zajjaj says the second could be omitted structurally but confirms parallel phrasing. Ibn Ashur says five emphases, including two min, fronting, restriction and reciprocal completion, repel pressure from Quraysh; he also gives the first clause priority. Abu Hayyan and Samin record a wording objection to Zamakhshari's singular ṣāḥibihi and Samin's repair by supplying 'each one.' Burhan names the reciprocal account clauses an inversion, comparing wives as each other's garment, mutual unlawfulness and night entering day; Itqan calls the form aks, a reversal of the first statement's parts in the second, and compares 57:6, 30:19, 2:187 and 60:10. Burhan also describes interwoven premise–consequence pairs."}, {"id": "6:52/q13/p2", "position": "The second clause chiefly exposes the chiefs' pretense that poor believers obstructed their access to the Prophet.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says no believer should lose rights to satisfy another; if chiefs truly sought faith they could attend without judging others, as 6:55 clarifies. He rejects reducing the two clauses to one statement that God judges all, because that makes the second redundant in context."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q14", "question": "How do the particles and fronted phrases in the account clauses work?", "turns_on": "The function of min, the grammatical status of fronted phrases, and whether the clauses are an interruption.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q14/p1", "position": "The first min is partitive and the second min emphatically broadens the negation.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya, Qurtubi, Abu Hayyan and Samin parse من حسابهم as partitive or circumstantial and من شيء as extra under negation. Samin lays out active or inactive ما, عليك as predicate or fronted predicate, and the possible raising of شيء. Abu Hayyan and Samin find treating من حسابك as a fronted circumstance weak because it precedes its semantic governor and owner; an explanatory analysis is possible. Ibn Ashur calls min extra for comprehensive denial."}, {"id": "6:52/q14/p2", "position": "The fronting of عليك and عليهم may honor the Prophet, emphasize the lack of obligation, or mark restriction.", "reasons": "Abu Hayyan and Samin say putting the Prophet first twice is honor and reciprocal framing, رد الأعجاز على الصدور, supported by proverb and poem. Ibn Ashur says negated indefinite subjects permit fronting; Kashshaf favors restriction, implying only God accounts for believers, comparing 37:47, while Ibn Ashur also permits simple emphasis because restriction fits imperfectly. He explains على as burden and discusses whether the genitive means the Prophet's reckoning or chiefs' assessment. As general word-order background rather than a direct parsing of 6:52, Jurjani argues that a meaningful placement consistently carries its benefit and illustrates with questions: verb-first asks whether an act occurred, while noun-first asks who did it."}, {"id": "6:52/q14/p3", "position": "The two clauses may interrupt the prohibition as parenthetical explanation.", "reasons": "Alusi says the clause supports the ban; Ibn Ashur says it can give the reason or invalidate the rationale for expulsion. Samin rejects making parenthesis depend on reference to polytheists; Abu Hayyan identifies the interruption before the ban's result."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q15", "question": "What governs the two subjunctive verbs after the account clauses?", "turns_on": "Which preceding negative or prohibition supplies the result, and whether the second verb answers that ban or coordinates with the first.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q15/p1", "position": "فتطردهم answers the preceding negation and فتكون answers the prohibition.", "reasons": "Akhfash, Tabari, Zajjaj, BaghaWi and others make the first consequence follow 'no account' and the second the ban. Abu Hayyan says the first denies an expulsion arising from that account; Samin rejects a reading where the visit occurs without conversation. Ibn Ashur allows the repeated expulsion clause to bridge the long interruption. Alusi rejects making the second denial govern if it would imply expulsion proper when accountability exists. Burhan describes two interwoven premise–consequence pairs: the ban on expulsion leads to avoiding injustice, and the reciprocal account clauses lead to the question of expelling them."}, {"id": "6:52/q15/p2", "position": "Both verbs follow the prohibition, warning that expulsion would make the Prophet unjust.", "reasons": "Akhfash reports this alternative; Abu Muslim parses both as consequences. {"id": "6:52/q16", "question": "What wrong would expelling the worshippers constitute?", "turns_on": "Whether the injustice falls on the poor, the Prophet, or is only the hypothetical consequence of a contemplated act.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q16/p1", "position": "It would wrong the believers who deserved welcome and honor.", "reasons": "Ibn Zayd calls their exclusion undeserved; Wahidi calls this sound. {"id": "6:52/q17", "question": "Did the Prophet sin or expel the poor before the warning?", "turns_on": "Whether reported consideration became actual expulsion or culpable disobedience.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q17/p1", "position": "He did not expel them; he considered a separate audience to attract the chiefs, and the warning is conditional.", "reasons": "Qurtubi, Alusi, Razi, Ibn al-Anbari and StudyQuran stress his intent to win converts; Razi says any mistaken judgment was forgoing the better course, not violating a duty. Ibn Ashur treats the warning likewise; reports vary between outright refusal and temporary willingness."}, {"id": "6:52/q17/p2", "position": "Critics of prophetic impeccability treat the incident as a sin and rebuke.", "reasons": "They allege he dismissed poor believers, invoking Noah's refusal to expel them (11:29), the command to follow prophets (6:90), worldly adornment (20:131), and 18:28. Razi rejects the inference by explaining the Prophet's intention and conditional wording."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q18", "question": "How does this verse connect to its surrounding passage and other Quranic episodes?", "turns_on": "Whether adjacent passages explain the command through context, analogous prophetic history, or later applications.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q18/p1", "position": "It follows the warning in 6:51 by commanding care for the devout, and continues through the trial and mercy statements in 6:53–54.", "reasons": "Kashshaf, Baydawi, Nasafi, Abu Hayyan and Ibn Ashur mark the turn from warning the heedless to honoring worshippers. Alusi allows, but does not require, simultaneous revelation of warning and prohibition. Ibn Ashur says renewed relative wording makes the entitlement to company explicit. Later verses test proud chiefs through poor believers and assure the latter of mercy; the question 'does God not know the grateful?' confirms His knowledge, TabRisi comparing Jarir's poetry. Wording of 6:53's outcome can mark consequence rather than purpose. Qatada, reported by Abd al-Razzaq, glosses God's testing some through others simply as mutual trial. Ibn Ishaq reports 6:52–54 together as the response to Quraysh's mockery of the poor companions. Khabbab's report in Ibn Majah joins the prohibition with 6:53–54 as God's favor to those believers."}, {"id": "6:52/q18/p2", "position": "It parallels Noah's refusal to dismiss low-status followers and God's command to remain with these believers in 18:28.", "reasons": "Zajjaj, Wahidi, Razi and Ibn Kathir compare 11:27 and 26:111–113, including laborers and craftsmen whose account belongs to God. Several reports make 18:28 the later command that the Prophet remain seated with the poor; StudyQuran also links the rebuke at 80:1–10 about a blind poor man. Khabbab's report in Ibn Majah also connects 18:28 to the Prophet's continued companionship with the poor believers."}, {"id": "6:52/q18/p3", "position": "Reports about adjacent verses or other figures may be applications rather than original occasions.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i treats claims about enemies of the Prophet's family as applications or inward readings due to the Meccan, single-period descent. Islahi notes Farahi's related discussion in his commentary on Abasa."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q19", "question": "What ethical rule does the prohibition teach?", "turns_on": "Whether the enduring addressees are faithful Muslims in the Prophet's company or all sincere seekers of God.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q19/p1", "position": "Sincere faith and devotion give the poor a claim to company and honor regardless of rank, dress or wealth.", "reasons": "Zajjaj says religion takes priority over status and leaders' pretext is exposed. Qushayri says God champions vulnerable believers and tells the Prophet to see inward longing beyond ragged clothes. Qurtubi and Kuranyolu forbid elevating people for finery or lineage. Islahi says prophetic concern for wayward people has limits when loyal companions would be neglected; Jesus' lost-sheep parable illustrates concern for returnees but cannot override this duty. Biqai says the mission seeks the afterlife, with no worldly gain in replacing poor with wealthy."}, {"id": "6:52/q19/p2", "position": "The enduring command also applies to people with incomplete beliefs: explain patiently rather than repel them.", "reasons": "Asad reads the wording beyond its occasion, applying it to anyone who believes in God and seeks grace; Kuranyolu says even a disputed occasion leaves a universal ethical lesson."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q20", "question": "What inward instruction is drawn from the verse?", "turns_on": "Different inward emphases on constant remembrance, self-effacement, and the disciplines of devotion.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q20/p1", "position": "Remain with sincere seekers, recognize inward rank, and cultivate uninterrupted remembrance.", "reasons": "Sulami transmits counsel to treat seekers gently and overlook slips, to keep the secret pure, and not distance those adorned with servanthood. Abu Bakr al-Farisi says sincere desire shows in continual remembrance and companionship with like seekers. Qushayri says God publicly attests to sincerity, while the seeker is driven by need and longing; a poem depicts crossing the wild without fear. Tustari describes intentions in every motion and stillness and distinctions between one who seeks and one whom God seeks, citing 42:38, 16:53 and angelic stations at 37:164."}, {"id": "6:52/q20/p2", "position": "Inward nearness may be beyond ordinary reward, fear, or intermediary accounts.", "reasons": "Qashani calls them complete people of unity whose hearts witness God, free of concern for reward, punishment, worldly status or even their own selves; expulsion interrupts this presence, while veiled observers see only poverty (70:23). Qushayri says reliance is on divine mercy rather than one's deeds, and their Master cares for those wholly devoted to Him."}, {"id": "6:52/q20/p3", "position": "Purity of sustenance, command keeping, sincere treatment of creatures and gratitude describe the servant's path.", "reasons": "Tustari says the ascetic has pure food, the devout works hardest at commands and prohibitions, and the beloved is most sincere to creatures; he calls a squandered life wasted. Qushayri contrasts gratitude and patience and quotes poems grateful even for a beloved's blame. Bursevi uses Bahlul's cemetery and hunger sayings, a king's parable of hidden beloveds and a Persian couplet on servants' lowliness."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q21", "question": "What reports and ancillary teachings are attached to keeping the poor near?", "turns_on": "Whether the ancillary material supplies a virtue report, a creed discussion, or merely reproduces the passage.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q21/p1", "position": "The Prophet honored the poor companions and warned against upsetting them.", "reasons": "Thalabi reports a promise that destitute migrants enter Paradise half a day, five hundred years, before wealthy believers; another report says the gathering resembles earlier prophets and righteous people. Ibn Kathir notes al-Hakim's grading of Sa'd's six-companion report by Bukhari and Muslim criteria and Ibn Hibban's route, and says Ibn Jarir transmitted a related report through Asbat."}, {"id": "6:52/q21/p2", "position": "A report condemns denial of divine decree as resembling Magians.", "reasons": "Tabataba'i reads it as condemning independent human creation of acts; Mu'tazilites invert its target to those affirming decree. {"id": "6:52/q24", "question": "What is the lexical range of wajh used in 'His face'?", "turns_on": "The word's ordinary physical sense, its extensions in Arabic, and its referent in this verse.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q24/p1", "position": "Its basic sense is an animal's face, through which facing ordinarily occurs.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi gives the basic sense and its explanation from the act of facing."}, {"id": "6:52/q24/p2", "position": "By extension it can mean an aspect, a leader or front, or the beginning of a day.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi lists these extensions; he reports al-Zajjaj's poetic evidence for wajh al-nahar as the day's beginning."}, {"id": "6:52/q24/p3", "position": "In this verse it denotes God's own self.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzi reports the exegetes' explanation, also grouping 18:28, 28:88, 30:38 and 76:9 with that sense."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q25", "question": "What dialectal substitutions for final weak sounds are recorded alongside al-ʿashiyy?", "turns_on": "Dialects and pause versus connected speech affect the realization of weak final sounds; only the Banū Saʿd example directly names al-ʿashiyy.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q25/p1", "position": "Banū Saʿd replace a weak final yāʾ with jīm at pause; a cited line says bi-l-ʿashj for bi-l-ʿashiyy.", "reasons": "Sibawayh gives Tamimj, ʿalj and ʿurbanj as further examples, with an unattributed poetic line also using al-baranj for al-barani."}, {"id": "6:52/q25/p2", "position": "Some dialects replace final alif with yāʾ or wāw at pause, while others retain alif; the familiar pronunciation retains it.", "reasons": "Sibawayh reports al-Khalil and Abu al-Khattab on rare Fuzara and Qays pausal yāʾ, prefers alif in pause and connection, reports Tayyiʾ's retained alif, and notes some Tayyiʾ speakers use a clearer wāw such as afʿaw."}, {"id": "6:52/q25/p3", "position": "Final yāʾ can alternate with hāʾ by dialect and by pause versus connection.", "reasons": "Sibawayh reports Banū Tamim's hādhihi in pause and hādhi in connection, while Hijaz and other Qays speakers retain hāʾ in both environments in contrast to Tayyiʾ's yāʾ; he says the latter is exceptional."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q26", "question": "What general weak-letter changes do the accompanying language notes describe?", "turns_on": "These are general morphological examples in the accompanying material; the notes do not apply them to a particular word of 6:52.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q26/p1", "position": "Medial wāw may be lengthened, hamzaed, changed to yāʾ, or preserved according to pattern and proximity to the word's end.", "reasons": "Sibawayh gives ghuwuran and al-quwwul, sawm/saym and qawl/qil, contrasts retained wāw in zuwwar and siwwam, describes analogical alternations in mashub/mashib and hawr/hayr, and gives retained wāw in tawil/tuwal, augmented patterns and fiʿlaʾ. He calls extension of the fiʿl change to fiʿlan and fiʿla irregular and contrasts lighter yāʾ. Sibawayh further traces wāw-to-yāʾ changes to kasra and a following alif or yāʾ-like sound in verbal nouns and plurals, including qiyām, siyāṭ, thiyāb and riyāḍ; a substituted yāʾ can persist in the plural. He distinguishes retained original wāw in sound-verb nouns, certain plurals, fuʿūl, augmented patterns and forms without the conditioning kasra; wāw after ḍamma may instead be hamzated. He marks thawra/thīra as nonproductive. Some speakers extend the fiʿl analogy irregularly to fiʿlān and fuʿlā."}, {"id": "6:52/q26/p2", "position": "Root-initial yāʾ is usually retained but changes in specified environments and analogical forms.", "reasons": "Sibawayh contrasts root yāʾ in yaʾisa and yabisa with wāw, cites retained yāʾ in yayiʾasu and yaybasu, its change to wāw after ḍamma, isolated analogies in vocatives, its change to tāʾ in iftiʿal, and preservation in afʿal; he limits nonproductive cases and reports Abu ʿAmr's hamza-to-yāʾ reading."}]}
{"id": "6:52/q27", "question": "How can Arabic noun forms denote an act or a concrete thing in the accompanying lexical notes?", "turns_on": "Sibawayh says the same outward pattern has several lexical functions that must be learned from usage.", "positions": [{"id": "6:52/q27/p1", "position": "A form's lexical meaning can be an action, an amount, its result, an agent or patient, or a collective member; the surface pattern alone does not decide.", "reasons": "Sibawayh discusses faʿul verbal nouns, waqud as burning or fuel, shibʿ and milʾ as amounts or acts, nouns with the same sense as their sources, unpredictable khars, kayla, qut and halab, mirya as milk quantity, laʿna and khalq as affected people or things, karaʿ and dhu tadruʾ as concrete referents, passive-result and agent senses, changed milk and pleasing usage, and collective members marked with feminine taʾ. These examples are ancillary and do not explicitly gloss a word in 6:52."}]}
{"id": "6:80/q01", "question": "What does the people's disputing with Abraham mean?", "turns_on": "Whether reciprocal morphology requires an actual exchange, allows one-sided contention, or identifies who initiated it.", "positions": [{"id": "6:80/q01/p1", "position": "They contended with him, each side advancing an argument or asking for proof.", "reasons": "Ibn Abbas and al-Rabi gloss it as quarrelling or disputing. Jishumi defines muḥājja as reciprocal presentation and demand for evidence. Ibn Atiyya derives it from ḥujja. Ibn Ashur prefers a real exchange and cites other Quranic debates with Abraham, including 21:52–56 and 26:72–73."}, {"id": "6:80/q01/p2", "position": "The reciprocal verb can describe an argument begun by the people while Abraham listens and then replies, or intensify a one-sided contention.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur allows the opponent's reception and response to justify reciprocal morphology even if only one side argues; the people's words are omitted to focus on Abraham's firmness."}, {"id": "6:80/q01/p3", "position": "The reciprocal form makes its grammatical subject the initiator.", "reasons": "Ibn Arafah applies this to 2:258, distinguishing Abraham's opening speech from Nimrod's opening of the debate; Ibn Ashur says grammarians do not establish this rule."}]}
{"id": "6:80/q02", "question": "What claims did Abraham's people raise in the dispute?", "turns_on": "The reports name inherited custom, rival deities, celestial powers, and threats; several sources give more than one.", "positions": [{"id": "6:80/q02/p1", "position": "They defended inherited worship and objected to the oneness of God.", "reasons": "Razi cites 43:23 and 38:5 for ancestral imitation and rejection of one God; Biqai says they insisted on inherited idols. Study Quran cites 21:53, 43:23 and 38:5. Abu Hayyan and Alusi describe traditional arguments as false."}, {"id": "6:80/q02/p2", "position": "They claimed their gods were better, asked Abraham to describe God, or urged him to worship another god.", "reasons": "Tabari reports the superiority claim; Ibn Ishaq reports the request to describe God. Ibn Jurayj reports invocation of other gods; al-Durr reports a call to worship one."}, {"id": "6:80/q02/p3", "position": "They argued for celestial bodies, idols, or created things as partners and causal powers.", "reasons": "Zajjaj and Abu Ishaq name stars, sun, moon, and idols; Qashani includes the alleged causal power of celestial and other created beings. The argument concerns divine oneness or attributes, as Ibn Ashur notes."}, {"id": "6:80/q02/p4", "position": "They threatened him with punishment or injury by their gods as part of their argument.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur says they mistook intimidation for proof. Tabatabai says fear of divine anger was their stronger motive for worship; his account has them press Abraham to accept their gods and reject God's lordship. Elmalili says their verbal and practical pressure aimed to win."}]}
